title: Life cycle archive
subtitle: Repair four mixed-up wildlife displays
objective: Describe the life cycles of a mammal, an amphibian, an insect and a bird using named examples.

sow.exactOutcome: Describe the life cycles of mammals, amphibians, insects and birds.
sow.alignment: Directly develops this stated outcome with secondary-age tasks at an upper-KS2 conceptual level. Support and stretch are flexible; this exemplar is not a claim of qualification approval.

priorLearning: Recognise rabbits, frogs, butterflies and birds as animals.
Know that offspring grow and that living things reproduce.
success: Order stages for four named animal examples.
Use growth, development and reproduction to explain arrows.
Use evidence to correct an over-general claim.

vocabulary.meaning: The stages in a living thing’s life, including reproduction that produces the next generation.
An immature stage with a different body form from the adult, such as a caterpillar.
The stage between larva and adult in insects with complete metamorphosis.
A major change in body form during development.
A young bird that has left the nest and is developing its flying skills.

equipment: Shared evidence page, one route page and exit page; pencil; optional paper stage labels and reusable arrows.
preparation: Print pages 1 and 5 plus one selected response page.
Read the named-species evidence before discussing whole animal groups. Prepare movable stage words if pupils benefit from sorting.
safety: Use paper evidence only. No animals, spawn, nests or eggs need to be collected or handled.
Keep reproduction discussion focused on the named wildlife examples; no personal or family disclosure is required.
practicalAlternative: All evidence and stage words are supplied. Pupils can point, sequence labels or explain aloud instead of drawing.

misconceptions.claim: A life cycle means the same adult turns into a baby again.
misconceptions.correction: Adults can reproduce to produce new individuals; the next generation begins.
misconceptions.check: Ask whether the egg after an adult is that adult or its offspring.

misconceptions.correction: Butterflies have a pupa; insects such as grasshoppers develop through nymph stages without a pupa.
misconceptions.check: Compare the monarch and grasshopper cards.

misconceptions.claim: A pupa is dead or simply resting.
misconceptions.correction: The living insect develops during the pupal stage.
misconceptions.check: Ask what changes between caterpillar and adult butterfly.

misconceptions.claim: Every mammal gives birth to live young.
misconceptions.correction: Most mammals do, including rabbits. Egg-laying mammals include the platypus.
misconceptions.check: Ask which card challenges the word every.

access.supported: Use supplied stage words, a matching table and short sentence frames.
access.standard: Create four accurate sequences with labelled development or reproduction arrows.
access.stretch: Repair a misleading guide using named counterexamples and model limitations.
access.regulation: Offer quiet sequencing, pointing, drawing, dictation or private writing. Use animal examples; pupils may pass and return to a question. Response routes follow current learning evidence.

slides.title: The wildlife archive is mixed up
body: Four displays have lost their stage labels.
Your job: repair the science, then explain the arrows.
slides.notes: Introduce a paper museum challenge. Pupils may work alone or with a partner. The goal is describing life cycles, not recalling precise ages or drawing realistic animals.

slides.title: What changes as animals grow?
body: R1. What are offspring?
R2. Is a young bird already a mature adult?
R3. Does one named example prove a rule for every animal?
slides.notes: R1 young produced by parents. R2 no; it still develops and matures. R3 no. Accept everyday words, then supply offspring and mature.

slides.title: I explain each frog arrow
body: Eggs hatch into tadpoles.
Tadpoles develop into froglets.
The adult-to-egg arrow means reproduction.
slides.notes: Think aloud: I follow the same individual from egg through tadpole and froglet to adult. At reproduction the arrow now links parents to offspring. I do not say the adult changes back into an egg. The timing and shapes are simplified.

visual.title: Common frog: changes across generations
visual.description:
Clockwise sequence: Eggs in water; Tadpole
grows and develops; Froglet
young frog; Adult frog
can reproduce. Adult → eggs means offspring,
not the adult becoming an egg.

elements.text:
Adult → eggs means offspring,
not the adult becoming an egg.

slides.title: I check for a pupal stage
body: The monarch has four named stages.
A caterpillar is a larva.
The pupa is alive and developing.
slides.notes: Shared I do time. Trace egg to larva to pupa to adult. Model the explanation: the caterpillar does not become a different species; its body develops. Use chrysalis for butterfly pupa. A cocoon is a covering made by some insects, not a synonym for every pupa.

visual.title: Monarch: complete metamorphosis
visual.description:
Clockwise sequence: Egg; Larva
caterpillar; Pupa
chrysalis; Adult butterfly. The pupa is a living development stage.
Reproduction produces the next generation.

elements.text:
The pupa is a living development stage.
Reproduction produces the next generation.

slides.title: I keep the animal name in the claim
body: Rabbit young are born alive and feed on milk.
Robin young hatch from eggs.
Both young animals grow and mature.
slides.notes: Shared I do time. Say: This describes a European rabbit and a robin. I retain their names because one species cannot establish a universal rule. A fledgling has left the nest but is not necessarily independent or reproductively mature.

visual.title: Two named animal sequences
visual.description: Two horizontal sequences compare development in European rabbits and robins. Rabbit young develop inside the mother and are born alive; young feed on milk. Robin young hatch from eggs, grow in the nest, then fledge and mature. Reproduction makes new offspring; these rows omit the connecting reproductive arrows.

elements.text: Rabbit and robin: two named life cycles
Mature adults can reproduce to produce new offspring.

slides.title: Repair three archive labels
body: Use page 1 cards A–F.
W1. The frog display says “egg → adult → tadpole → froglet”.
Repair it and explain two arrows.
slides.notes: Use movable labels or the HTML prediction/test panel. Correct order egg→tadpole→froglet→adult; reproduction then produces eggs of the next generation. Ask where the identity changes from parent to offspring.

rows: All mammals give live birth; all insects have a pupa
table.caption: Authored archive errors for pupils to repair.

slides.title: Recover the missing stage
body: W2. The monarch display has lost its pupa.
Where should it go?
Explain why “it does nothing” is misleading.
slides.notes: Shared We do time. Place pupa between larva and adult. Development occurs in this living stage. Choose evidence, test, then explain using card B; paper route gives the same evidence.
slides.reveal: Egg → larva → pupa → adult. The pupa is alive and developing.

slides.title: Challenge the word all
body: W3. Test both guide claims using cards E and F.
Name a counterexample for each.
Write a more careful statement.
slides.notes: Shared We do time. Grasshopper challenges all insects have a pupa. Platypus challenges all mammals give live birth. Better claims: monarch butterflies have a pupal stage; rabbits give live birth, but some mammals lay eggs. Do not change mammal classification because a species lays eggs.

slides.title: What does the returning arrow mean?
body: In a cycle, an arrow goes from an adult to eggs.
slides.notes: A incorrect: one adult does not become its own egg. B correct: reproduction produces a new generation. C incorrect: stage positions do not set calendar duration. Re-teach with two different coloured tokens for parent and offspring.

options.text: The same adult turns into an egg.
options.feedback: The egg is a new individual, not the adult changing back.
The arrow links parents to new offspring.

options.text: Every stage takes exactly the same time.
options.feedback: A life-cycle diagram shows order; equal spacing does not mean equal time.

slides.title: Build a reliable display
body: Choose supported, standard or stretch.
Use page 1 as your evidence archive.
Include all four core animal examples.
slides.notes: Select one route. Supported pupils complete key stage words and matching; standard pupils make four sequences; stretch pupils combine the four core sequences with counterexamples. Dictated stage explanations can count as independent evidence.

slides.title: Check what your arrows say
body: Hatching, growth and development are not the same as reproduction.
Name the species.
Mark which arrow leads to offspring.
slides.notes: Shared You do time. Point to a single arrow and ask what changes. Prompt with the evidence card rather than giving the next stage. No requirement to copy scientific species names.

slides.title: An audience checks the display
body: L1. Show or describe one sequence.
Audience: “Which arrow starts the next generation?”
Revise one unclear label.
slides.notes: Use a paired check, teacher conference or private self-check. Look for order, named species and meaning of the reproductive arrow. Pupils need not perform publicly.

slides.title: A smaller animal is not always an adult
body: A fledgling robin has left the nest.
A froglet looks like a small frog.
Both still develop and mature.
slides.notes: Shared review time. Ask pupils to explain why leaving a nest or changing shape is not automatically the same as reproductive maturity. Do not add age thresholds.

slides.title: Three final archive checks
body: E1. Name the monarch stage after larva.
E2. Name a young stage in the frog or robin cycle.
E3. Explain the adult-to-offspring link.
slides.notes: E1 pupa/chrysalis. E2 tadpole, froglet, nestling or fledgling, matched to the named species. E3 reproduction produces new individuals. Take a spoken, written or pointed response.

slides.title: Choose a useful next step
body: Stage order • explanation of an arrow • a careful claim.
slides.notes: Shared exit time. Use the response to plan the scheme’s following comparison lesson. A confidence choice is not scored as scientific attainment.

pupilPages.title: Shared evidence for the life cycle archive
pupilPages.intro: These source-based summaries describe named animals. They are not records from a classroom animal investigation.

cards.title: A Common frog | amphibian
cards.text: Eggs are laid in water. Tadpoles hatch, grow legs and absorb their tails as they become froglets. Froglets grow and mature into adults. Reproduction produces new eggs.

cards.title: B Monarch | insect
cards.text: Egg → larva (caterpillar) → pupa (chrysalis) → adult butterfly. The pupa is alive and developing. Mature adults can reproduce and produce offspring.

cards.title: C European rabbit | mammal
cards.text: Young develop inside the mother and are born alive. Newborn kits feed on milk, grow into young rabbits and mature into adults. Reproduction produces new offspring.

cards.title: D Robin | bird
cards.text: Egg → nestling chick → fledgling → mature adult. The embryo develops inside the egg. A fledgling is still a young bird. Adults can reproduce and produce eggs.

cards.title: E Grasshopper | insect
cards.text: Egg → nymph → adult. Nymphs grow and shed their outer skeleton several times. There is no pupal stage in this sequence.

cards.title: F Platypus | mammal
cards.text: A platypus lays eggs. Young hatch and feed on milk from their mother. This is a mammal that lays eggs instead of giving birth to live young.

blocks.text: W1. Repair “egg → adult → tadpole → froglet”. Explain two arrows in the common-frog cycle.
W2. The monarch display says “egg → larva → adult”. Restore the missing stage and explain what happens in it.
W3. Test “all insects have a pupa” and “all mammals give live birth”. Use E and F to name a counterexample for each. Say, point, move labels or write on paper.

pupilPages.title: Supported route for the archive
pupilPages.intro: Use cards A–D. Complete the missing stage, then explain the reproduction link.

blocks.text: S1. Complete the missing stage in each row.

rows: Develops inside mother → newborn kit → young rabbit → ______

blocks.text: Stage bank: tadpole / pupa / mature adult / fledgling.

blocks.prompt: S2. Which named animal has young that are born alive?
S3. Complete: Reproduction produces new ______. The adult does not become its own egg.
S4. Name one arrow that shows growth or development. Explain what changes.

pupilPages.title: Standard route for the archive
pupilPages.intro: Use cards A–D to write or sketch four labelled stage sequences. Use arrows; realistic drawing is unnecessary.

blocks.prompt: N1. Common frog: give the stages and label the reproductive link.
N2. Monarch: give the stages and explain what happens in the pupa.
N3. European rabbit: begin before birth, then describe the young and adult stages.
N4. Robin: show the egg, nestling, fledgling and mature adult stages.
N5. Why does a circular diagram not mean that the same individual lives again?

pupilPages.title: Stretch route for the archive
pupilPages.intro: Use all six cards. Your guide must explain the four core examples and avoid false group rules.

blocks.prompt: T1. Give one correct stage sequence for each of A–D. Add a sentence explaining the link between adult and offspring.
T2. Repair “all insects have a pupa” and “all mammals give live birth”. Use a named counterexample for each.
T3. A diagram spaces all stages equally. Can you infer how long each lasts? Explain and suggest evidence you would need.
T4. Explain why a fledgling robin and a froglet are young stages even though each resembles an adult.

pupilPages.title: Exit and reflection for the archive
pupilPages.intro: Answer independently using words, pointing or a short spoken explanation.

blocks.prompt: E1. Name the monarch stage after larva.
E2. Name a young stage for either the common frog or the robin. State which animal.
E3. Explain how reproduction links one generation with the next.
L1. Which label or arrow did your audience help you improve?

choices: Use a named example to test a claim.

answers.label: R1–R3
answers.answer: R1 offspring are young produced by parents. R2 a young bird is not yet a mature adult. R3 one species cannot establish a universal rule for every animal.

answers.label: W1–W3
answers.answer: W1 egg→tadpole→froglet→adult. Hatching links egg and tadpole; development produces legs and the froglet body; growth and maturation lead to the adult. Reproduction produces the next generation of eggs. W2 pupa belongs between larva and adult; it is a living stage during which the body develops. W3 grasshopper has no pupa; platypus lays eggs but is a mammal. Accept narrower true statements such as “monarchs have a pupal stage” and “rabbits give live birth; some mammals lay eggs”.

answers.label: Hinge A–C
answers.answer: A incorrect: an adult does not turn into its own egg. B correct: reproduction produces new individuals. C incorrect: diagram spacing does not measure elapsed time.

answers.label: S1–S4
answers.answer: S1 missing words in row order: tadpole; pupa; mature adult; fledgling. S2 European rabbit. S3 offspring or young. S4 examples: tadpole develops legs and absorbs its tail; kit grows into a young rabbit; nestling develops feathers and later fledges. Do not accept an adult turning back into its own egg.

answers.label: N1–N5
answers.answer: N1 egg→tadpole→froglet→adult; reproductive link leads to new eggs. N2 egg→larva/caterpillar→pupa/chrysalis→adult; living development occurs in the pupa. N3 development inside mother→newborn kit fed on milk→growing young rabbit→mature adult; adults can produce offspring. N4 egg→nestling→fledgling→mature adult; adults can produce new eggs. N5 the circular representation joins generations through reproduction; it does not reverse one individual’s age.

answers.label: T1–T4
answers.answer: T1 use the four accurate N1–N4 sequences and state that reproduction produces new offspring. T2 grasshopper counterexample shows not every insect has a pupa; platypus counterexample shows not every mammal gives live birth. T3 equal diagram spacing gives no duration; dated observations following identified individuals under recorded conditions would provide timing evidence. T4 resemblance or leaving a nest does not establish reproductive maturity; each still grows and develops. Accept other accurate model limitations, including omitted mortality and individual variation.

answers.label: E1–E3 and L1
answers.answer: E1 pupa or chrysalis. E2 a correctly paired example: common-frog tadpole/froglet or robin nestling/fledgling. E3 reproduction produces new individuals of the next generation. L1 is a reflection, not a test of personal disclosure.

answers.label: Success and response to misconceptions
answers.answer: Secure: ordered cycles for all four named examples and an explanation of reproduction. Re-teach jumbled stages with movable labels. Use separate parent and offspring tokens if pupils reverse an individual’s age. Test a broad group claim with one named counterexample; extra species need not be memorised.

teacherNotes: 40 minutes: opening 2; retrieval 3; I do 8; We do 8; hinge 3; You do 10; review 4; exit 2. Zero-minute slides share their stage time.
Supply shared page 1, one selected route page 2, 3 or 4, and page 5. Do not require all three routes. An independent spoken explanation can be recorded verbatim by an adult.

Interactive We do: predict a sequence, test the annotated SVG evidence, then explain or revise. Use Pause or Reset as needed. Paper W1–W3 assesses the same reasoning within the existing eight minutes.
The diagrams show selected stages and links, not anatomy, actual relative sizes or elapsed time. Some individuals die before reproducing; a cycle diagram is not a guarantee of survival.

Core assessment describes four named life cycles. Counterexamples support careful reasoning and bridge to next week’s comparison outcome; their technical classification details are optional extension.
